problems.title: Integer part of fractional powers
problems.question: Find floor(2^(4/3)+2^(1/3)).
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
steps: 1<cube-root(2)<4/3 because 1<2<64/27. Multiplying by 3 gives a value strictly between 3 and 4, so its floor is 3.

problems.title: Smallest term of a quadratic sequence
problems.question: Find the smallest term of aₙ=n²−8n+199 for n=1,2,… .
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
steps: The minimum occurs at integer index n=4 and equals 183.

problems.title: Inradius and circumradius of a regular polygon
problems.question: Find inradius/circumradius for a regular n-gon.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: The centre, a vertex and an adjacent side midpoint form a right triangle with centre angle 180°/n.
steps: The inradius is the adjacent leg and circumradius the hypotenuse, so their ratio is cos(180°/n).

problems.title: Sector area with a radian angle
problems.question: A sector has radius 1 and central angle 0.1 radians. Find its area.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: $S=R^2\theta/2$ when θ is in radians.
steps: S=1²×0.1/2=0.05. No extra factor of π is needed.

problems.title: An equilateral triangle’s circumcircle area
problems.question: An equilateral triangle has area 3√3. Find its circumcircle area.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: Triangle area $=s^2\sqrt3/4$ and circumradius $=s/\sqrt3$.
steps: s²=12, so R²=s²/3=4. The circle area is 4π.

problems.title: Three congruences with a common remainder
problems.question: Find the least integer n>1 such that n≡1 modulo 5,7,11.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: n−1 must be a positive common multiple of 5,7,11.
steps: Their least common multiple is 5×7×11=385. Thus n=386.

problems.title: Cancel a common odd-root factor
problems.question: Simplify [seventh-root(x²y⁵)−seventh-root(x³y³)−seventh-root(x⁴y²)]/[seventh-root(xy³)−seventh-root(x²y)−seventh-root(x³)].
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: For real odd roots, multiplication holds for either sign. Factor out $\sqrt[7]{xy^2}$ from the numerator.
steps: Multiplying each denominator term by seventh-root(xy²) gives its corresponding numerator term exactly.
Thus the quotient is seventh-root(xy²), on the original domain where the denominator is nonzero.

problems.title: Conditions for two negative quadratic roots
problems.question: Which conditions exactly characterize two distinct negative roots of ax²−bx+c=0?
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: Vieta gives sum $b/a$ and product $c/a$; distinct real roots require D>0.
steps: Both roots are negative iff their sum is negative and product positive. These are ab<0 and ac>0, automatically ensuring a≠0.
Together the full conditions are D>0,ac>0,ab<0.

problems.title: Circle area ratio from a shared chord
problems.question: The same chord subtends 90° in one circle and 120° in another. Find the smaller/larger disk-area ratio.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: Chord $c=2R\sin(\theta/2)$.
steps: The radii are c/√2 for 90° and c/√3 for 120°. Their squared radii, and hence areas, have ratio 3:2.
Thus the smaller disk’s area divided by the larger is 2/3; the reverse ordered ratio is 3/2.

problems.title: Area of an intersection lens
problems.question: Two circles share a chord of length 6, subtending 90°,120°. Their centre segment crosses the chord. Find intersection area.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: Each minor circular segment has area $R^2(\theta-\sin\theta)/2$ with radians θ.
steps: The squared radii are 18 and 12. With centres on opposite sides of the common chord, the lens is the sum of the two minor segments.
Adding gives 8.5π−9−3√3.

problems.title: A quotient of cubic half-powers
problems.question: Simplify (x^1.5−y^1.5)/(x^0.5−y^0.5) for admissible real inputs.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: Put $u=\sqrt x,v=\sqrt y$; $(u^3-v^3)/(u-v)=u^2+uv+v^2$.
steps: The result is x+√(xy)+y. Original restrictions are x,y≥0 and x≠y.

problems.title: Identify the increasing sequence
problems.question: Which of aₙ=n²−20n+199,bₙ=(−1)ⁿ/n,cₙ=(2n+1)/(n+2) is increasing for all positive integer indices?
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
steps: cₙ increases as its positive subtracted fraction decreases. aₙ first decreases and then increases, while bₙ alternates signs and is not increasing.

problems.title: Identify upper-bounded sequences
problems.question: Which of aₙ=n²−20n+199,bₙ=(−1)ⁿ/n,cₙ=(2n+1)/(n+2) are bounded above?
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
steps: aₙ is not bounded above. The bounds 1 and 2 suffice for bₙ and cₙ respectively.

problems.title: A rhombus angle from two areas
problems.question: A rhombus has area 8/π and its incircle area is 1. Find the acute angle.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: $r^2=1/\pi$, rhombus area $=2rs=s^2\sin\alpha$.
steps: 2rs=8/π gives s=4/√π. Then sinα=2r/s=1/2. The acute solution is α=30°.

problems.title: Equal numbers in different units
problems.question: A circle circumference measured in cm numerically equals its disk area measured in m². Find radius in dm.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: If radius is R cm, circumference $=2\pi R$ cm and area $=\pi R^2/10000$ m².
steps: Equating numbers and canceling πR>0 gives 2=R/10000, so R=20000 cm. Divide by 10 to get 2000 dm.

problems.title: A quadratic inequality with positive solutions only
problems.question: How many integer a make the nonempty solution set of x²−6x+a≤0 consist only of positive numbers?
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: The solution interval is $[3-\sqrt{9-a},3+\sqrt{9-a}]$ when a≤9.
steps: Nonemptiness requires a≤9. Its left endpoint is strictly positive iff √(9−a)<3, or a>0.
Thus integers a=1,…,9 give nine values. At a=9 the single solution x=3 is allowed.
problems.note: The count assumes the inequality has at least one solution. If an empty solution set is allowed to count as “only positive solutions,” every a>9 also qualifies, giving infinitely many integer parameters.

problems.title: A nested exponent in lowest terms
problems.question: For x>0, seventh-root[x⁶·fifth-root(x⁴·cube-root(x²))]=x^(m/n), with coprime positive integers m,n. Find n−m.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: Work from the innermost root outward; roots divide exponents.
steps: The fifth-root part has exponent (4+2/3)/5=14/15. The outer exponent is (6+14/15)/7=104/105.
104 and 105 are coprime, so n−m=105−104=1.

problems.title: Independent modular restrictions on a pair
problems.question: Count positive integers x,y<15 with 4x+5y≡2 mod5 and ≡1 mod4.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: The first reduces to x≡3 mod5; the second to y≡1 mod4.
steps: Allowed x are 3,8,13 and allowed y are 1,5,9,13. Independent choices give 3×4=12 ordered pairs.

problems.title: Area outside six overlapping disks in a hexagon
problems.question: On each side of a regular hexagon of side 2, draw a disk with that side as diameter. Find the hexagon area outside all six disks.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: Hexagon area $=6\sqrt3$; each inside half-disk has area π/2. Account for pairwise overlaps.
steps: Adjacent disk centres are √3 apart and each radius is 1. Their overlap lens has area 2(π/6−√3/4)=π/3−√3/2.
There are six such lenses. Nonadjacent disks do not overlap in positive area, so there are no triple-overlap regions. The covered hexagon area is 3π−6(π/3−√3/2)=π+3√3.
Subtract from 6√3 to obtain 3√3−π.

problems.title: Three-disk intersection at equilateral vertices
problems.question: An equilateral triangle has side √2. Three disks centred at its vertices have radius √2. Find their common intersection area.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: The intersection is a Reuleaux triangle; area = three 60° sectors minus twice the equilateral triangle area.
steps: For side s, the result is 3(πs²/6)−2(√3s²/4)=s²(π−√3)/2. With s²=2 it becomes π−√3.

problems.title: A recurrence from a quadratic index formula
problems.question: Find a recurrence for aₙ=n²−n, n=1,2,… .
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
steps: The difference simplifies to 2n, and a₁=0. Thus aₙ₊₁=aₙ+2n.

problems.title: Check which claims hold for every index
problems.question: I: 2^(2n)3^(n+1)+4·5ⁿ is divisible by 7. II: 1+…+n+(n+1)=(n²+3n−2)/2. III: n(n+1)>2^(n−1). Which hold for every positive integer n?
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: Reduce powers modulo 7; use the arithmetic-sum formula and counterexamples.
steps: I is 3·12ⁿ+4·5ⁿ≡7·5ⁿ≡0 mod7, so it always holds.
II’s correct sum is (n+1)(n+2)/2=(n²+3n+2)/2, not the printed expression. III fails at n=7 because 56<64.

problems.title: Floor conditions on two quadratic roots
problems.question: Find a such that ax²+(2a−5)x−1=0 has roots with floors −1 and 0.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: The roots must lie in $[-1,0)$ and $(0,1)$; their negative product forces a>0.
steps: f(0)=−1<0, so an upward quadratic has one root on either side of zero. The negative root is at least −1 iff f(−1)=4−a≥0.
The positive root is strictly below 1 iff f(1)=3a−6>0. Combining gives a≤4 and a>2.

problems.title: Directions of chords in a regular polygon
problems.question: In a regular n-gon, the lines A₁₂Aₙ₋₁ and A₂A₁₅ form a 9° angle. Which listed n is possible?
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: A chord’s direction is half the sum of its endpoint angular positions, plus 90° modulo 180°.
steps: The difference of the endpoint-index sums is (12+n−1)−(2+15)=n−6. Thus the line-direction difference is 180°−1080°/n, equivalent to 1080°/n modulo 180°.
For n≥16 this is below 90°, so the required smaller angle gives 1080°/n=9°. Hence n=120.

problems.title: Sum of distances to all regular-polygon sides
problems.question: A regular decagon has side 2. K lies on diagonal A₁A₄ with A₁K:KA₄=2:3. Find the sum of its perpendicular distances to all ten side lines.
problems.idea: Use exact identities or geometric formulas and check the original assumptions.
formulas: Join interior point K to all vertices: total area $=(s/2)\sum d_i$. Also polygon area $=nsr/2$.
steps: Equate the area formulas to get Σdᵢ=nr, independent of the location of K.
For side s=2, apothem r=s/[2tan18°]=cot18°. Thus the sum is 10cot18°. The given diagonal division does not affect it.
